3.9 Equity Valuation I: Dividend Discount Models

This content was generated by AI. It may contain errors and is not investment advice.

A stock’s intrinsic value

Section titled “A stock’s intrinsic value”

A bond is worth the present value of its promised cash flows (3.3 Bond Pricing). A stock has no promised cash flows; shareholders receive dividends and the price at which they later sell. Let DtD_tDt​ be the dividend per share at the end of year ttt, PtP_tPt​ the price, and rrr the expected return shareholders require. An investor holding for one year will pay

P0=D1+P11+rP_0 = \frac{D_1 + P_1}{1 + r}P0​=1+rD1​+P1​​

The buyer a year later prices the stock the same way: P1=D2+P21+rP_1 = \frac{D_2 + P_2}{1 + r}P1​=1+rD2​+P2​​. Substituting again and again, as long as PT(1+r)T\frac{P_T}{(1 + r)^T}(1+r)TPT​​ goes to 0 as TTT grows, we get

P0=∑t=1∞Dt(1+r)tP_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{D_t}{(1 + r)^t}P0​=t=1∑∞​(1+r)tDt​​

A stock’s intrinsic value is the present value of its expected future dividends; this is the dividend discount model (DDM). The result is the same however long the investor plans to hold: the price a short-term investor sells at depends on the dividends the next buyer expects.

The discount rate rrr is the expected return shareholders require given the stock’s risk, the cost of equity. It is usually above the company’s borrowing rate, because shareholders are paid after creditors and bear more risk. How to set it from risk is the subject of 4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM); this lesson takes it as given.

Check C1
A profitable company announces that it will never pay dividends, never return cash to shareholders through buybacks or in any other way, and will never be acquired or liquidated. By the dividend discount model, what is its stock worth?
Book value is capital put in the past, but shareholders can never get it back.
If profits stay in the company and are never passed to shareholders in any way, what do shareholders get from them?
The next buyer faces the same problem: he never gets cash either. By the dividend discount model, what ultimately supports this chain of prices?

The Gordon growth model

Section titled “The Gordon growth model”

Estimating every future dividend separately is not realistic. The simplest assumption is that dividends grow forever at a constant rate ggg: Dt=D1(1+g)t−1D_t = D_1(1 + g)^{t-1}Dt​=D1​(1+g)t−1. The dividends are then a growing perpetuity, and when g<rg < rg<r (derivation in Exercises Question 1):

P0=D1r−gP_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g}P0​=r−gD1​​

This is the Gordon growth model. Rewritten,

r=D1P0+gr = \frac{D_1}{P_0} + gr=P0​D1​​+g

the shareholder’s expected return equals the dividend yield plus the growth rate of dividends.

The denominator of the formula is r−gr - gr−g, the difference of two uncertain numbers. When ggg is close to rrr the denominator is small, and a small change in ggg or rrr changes the price a lot. Figure 2-1 plots this relation.

Check C2
In Figure 2-1, set the required return to 9%. First raise growth from 1% to 2%, then raise it from 7% to 8%. Comparing the two percentage changes in price:
The price is D1r−g\frac{D_1}{r - g}r−gD1​​. Growth rises by 1 point both times, but does the denominator change by the same proportion?
Work out by what percentage the denominator r−gr - gr−g changes each time.
Try it in the figure: is the price change small when growth is close to 9%?

Where growth comes from

Section titled “Where growth comes from”

A company pays part of its net income to shareholders as dividends and keeps the rest to reinvest. Dividends as a share of net income is the payout ratio; the share kept, bbb, is the retention ratio.

Retained profit increases shareholders’ equity. If the company earns the same ROE (return on equity) on the new equity, and neither raises its debt ratio nor issues new shares, then profit, dividends and equity all grow at the same rate:

g=b×ROEg = b \times \text{ROE}g=b×ROE

This is the sustainable growth rate.

Let E1E_1E1​ be next year’s earnings per share. If the company paid out all its profit and never grew, the price would be a perpetuity, E1r\frac{E_1}{r}rE1​​. The part of the actual price above this comes from what the market expects of the company’s future investments; it is the present value of growth opportunities (PVGO):

P0=E1r+PVGOP_0 = \frac{E_1}{r} + \text{PVGO}P0​=rE1​​+PVGO

Does keeping profit to invest always raise the price? Check C3 asks about this.

Check C3
If a company retains more of its profit to reinvest and its growth rate rises as a result, its stock price must go up.
Think: retained profit goes into new investment. How does the return on that investment, compared with what shareholders could earn themselves (the cost of equity), affect the price?

Multistage models

Section titled “Multistage models”

Many companies grow fast now but cannot grow that fast forever. A multistage model estimates the dividends of the first few years one by one, and then assumes that from year TTT on they grow at a lower rate gLg_LgL​ that can last forever (Exercises Question 4):

P0=∑t=1TDt(1+r)t+PT(1+r)T,PT=DT+1r−gLP_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{D_t}{(1 + r)^t} + \frac{P_T}{(1 + r)^T}, \qquad P_T = \frac{D_{T+1}}{r - g_L}P0​=t=1∑T​(1+r)tDt​​+(1+r)TPT​​,PT​=r−gL​DT+1​​

PTP_TPT​ is called the terminal value.

Many companies pay no dividends, or return cash to shareholders mainly through buybacks. Buybacks reduce the number of shares, so each remaining shareholder gets more future cash per share. One can then replace dividends with all the cash shareholders receive (dividends plus buybacks), value the company’s equity as a whole and divide by today’s number of shares; or estimate directly the cash flow the company generates for all its investors, the method of 3.10 Equity Valuation II: Discounted Free Cash Flow.

The conclusions of a DDM are very sensitive to its assumptions: the cost of equity and the long-run growth rate can only be estimated, and small changes in them change the value a lot. So a valuation should be read as a range, not as a precise number.

Check C4
A company's dividends have grown 12% a year in recent years, and its cost of equity is 9%. Plugging g=12%g = 12\%g=12% into the Gordon formula gives a negative price, which shows that the stock has no value.
Think: under what condition is the Gordon formula derived? Does this growth rate meet it? Can a company grow at 12% forever?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • A stock’s intrinsic value is the present value of expected future dividends at the cost of equity: P0=∑t=1∞Dt(1+r)tP_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{D_t}{(1 + r)^t}P0​=∑t=1∞​(1+r)tDt​​.
  • Gordon growth model: P0=D1r−gP_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g}P0​=r−gD1​​, which requires g<rg < rg<r; expected return r=D1P0+gr = \frac{D_1}{P_0} + gr=P0​D1​​+g. The price is very sensitive to r−gr - gr−g.
  • Sustainable growth rate g=b×ROEg = b \times \text{ROE}g=b×ROE; P0=E1r+PVGOP_0 = \frac{E_1}{r} + \text{PVGO}P0​=rE1​​+PVGO.
  • Multistage models estimate dividends year by year during high growth and capture later value in a terminal value; companies that pay no dividends or mainly buy back shares can be valued with all the cash shareholders receive.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1 ★
(a) From P0=∑t=1∞D1(1+g)t−1(1+r)tP_0 = \sum_{t=1}^{\infty} \frac{D_1(1 + g)^{t-1}}{(1 + r)^t}P0​=∑t=1∞​(1+r)tD1​(1+g)t−1​, derive P0=D1r−gP_0 = \frac{D_1}{r - g}P0​=r−gD1​​ and explain why g<rg < rg<r is needed. Show that the price a year later is P1=P0(1+g)P_1 = P_0(1 + g)P1​=P0​(1+g).
(b) A stock market has a dividend yield of 2%, and investors expect dividends to grow 5% a year. By the Gordon model, what is the expected return? If prices then double while dividends and growth expectations stay the same, what does the expected return become? What does this mean for investors who buy when valuations are high?
Question 2
A company has just paid a dividend of D0=1D_0 = 1D0​=1 per share. Dividends are expected to grow 15% a year for the next 5 years and 4% a year forever after. The cost of equity is 9%.
(a) Use a two-stage model to find the stock's value. What percentage of the total value is the present value of the terminal value?
(b) If second-stage growth were 5% instead of 4%, would the value change a lot? What does this show? (A qualitative answer is enough.)
Question 3
(a) A company will earn 4 per share next year; its cost of equity is 10% and its price is 60. What is PVGO? What percentage of the price is it?
(b) Another company earns an ROE of 15% on its existing business, will also earn 4 per share next year, and has a cost of equity of 10%. It plans to retain 50% of its profit for new projects, but the new projects earn only 8%. Management says: "Our ROE is 15%, above the cost of equity, so we should retain more profit." Using the return on the new projects, find the growth rate and the price, and compare with the price if all profit were paid out with no growth. What is wrong with management's argument?
Question 4
A stock is priced at 80, next year's expected dividend is 3.2, and the cost of equity is 9%.
(a) By the Gordon model, what long-run dividend growth rate does the market imply?
(b) Suppose the economy's long-run nominal growth rate is about 4%. Why can a company's dividends not grow faster than the economy forever? Is the implied growth rate reasonable?
